newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish prosecutor probes top general's accusations.
newsitem.headline: Polish prosecutor probes top general's accusations.

text.p: Polish military prosecutors on Tuesday began examining allegations by the dismissed chief of the armed forces that the security service had been deployed against him for political purposes.

The complaint was filed to the Supreme Military Prosecutor by General Tadeusz Wilecki on Monday, just before he was dismissed from the post of armed forces chief-of-staff after a row with the ruling ex-communist party.
Wilecki told public radio on Monday he had notified the prosecutor about a crime involving "misuse of the security service for political needs of certain politicians."
The military prosecutors now have 30 days to decide whether to open a full investigation or drop the case, their spokesman Janusz Palus said.
"The procedure which has been launched will be mainly aimed at checking facts and gathering more data," Palus told Reuters. He declined to give details, saying the investigation was secret.

Since the 1989 fall of communism, which was supposed to end the abuse of the security service by those in power, the ex-communists and groups rooted in the Solidarity movement have often accused one another of politicising the service.
Ex-communist President Aleksander Kwasniewski, who dismissed the general, and Defense Minister Stanislaw Dobrzanski both played down Wilecki's accusations.
"The motion is not very strong," Dobrzanski told public radio.
Kwasniewski earlier said he had seen the general's complaint, which concerned "improper actions by military intelligence against Wilecki." The president did not elaborate.
Kwasniewski fired Wilecki saying he needed a new chief-of-staff to complete reforms of the military before the country's accession to NATO, which Poland hopes to join in 1999.
The president also suggested the general had to go because of his rows with the defence ministry.

Some Western diplomats have said Wilecki tried to entrench his powers at the expense of the defence ministry and was therefore an obstacle to the introduction of high standards of civilian control required by NATO from new members.

But many opposition politicians alleged that Wilecki's dismissal was meant to increase the influence of ex-communists, co-ruling with the Polish Peasant party (PSL) since 1993, over the military before this year's parliamentary elections.
